meeting_header:
Date: 2025-09-30
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Rao (BeaconMed), Carlos Mendes (BeaconMed Infra), Aisha Khan (BeaconMed Sec), Tom Greer (BeaconMed SRE)
summary: Technical deep dive focused on multi-region routing behavior for private (VPC/on-prem) deployments. Primary goals: design an interruption-tolerant routing policy that minimizes cold-start costs, preserves KV-cache locality where possible, defines quantization fallback lanes for capacity-constrained regions, and documents an evacuation (failover) runbook for BeaconMed's private clusters. Discussed tradeoffs between latency and cost, warmup sequencing, and audit requirements for cross-region fallbacks.
topics: routing policy primitives (penalty, sticky sessions, region weight)
quantization fallback lanes and quality monitoring
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: ok everyone thanks for joining, we've got about 45 minutes, um, and the objective is to walk through a practical evacuation / fallback design for BeaconMed's private deployment, call it an "evacuation routing" pattern, uh, we'll talk KV warmup and batching, ethan will walk some runtime heuristics.
[00:00:15] Dr. Priya Rao: Thanks Maya. High level we run a private cluster in GCP us-west-2, latency sensitive patient triage workflows, p95 under 220ms is our target, we can't send PHI to public endpoints without a legal sign-off.
[00:00:28] Ethan Park: got it. Quick question — when you say "private cluster" is it full air-gapped on-prem or VPC peered?
[00:00:34] Carlos Mendes: It's VPC with a private control plane, we use Shared VPC with firewall rules; there's a backup colo stack in us-east for disaster recovery but we haven't activated cross-region routing in production.
[00:00:44] Maya Chen: perfect, so the two common evacuation strategies are: 1) active-active with sticky session routing and best-effort KV sync, 2) active-primary with a controlled evacuation to secondary region where we accept higher latency but maintain data controls. We proposed a middle ground: policy-based "evacuation lane" where traffic is gradually redirected and caching warmups are sequenced to reduce cold-token costs.
[00:01:10] Tom Greer: can you define "warmup sequenced"? sounds expensive.
[00:01:14] Ethan Park: yeah so instead of indiscriminately pre-warming whole model instances (which costs $$$), we do prioritized prefix warmup based on recent traffic heuristics — e.g., top 20 request prefixes in the last 6 hours, then expand. This works well with KV-cache because we keep hot KV segments local and stream in other parts lazily.
[00:01:33] Aisha Khan: but any cross-region fallback must be logged and auditable. We have to ensure KMS keys are properly scoped.
[00:01:38] Maya Chen: absolutely — we've baked in audit hooks and KMS key usage notes for private deployments. We can restrict fallback lanes to encrypted tunnels and ensure no raw PHI leaves region unless allowed.
[00:01:50] [00:02:00] Ethan Park: quick segue to runtime heuristics: the serving runtime has three knobs for evacuation — route penalty, sticky TTL, and quantization band. Route penalty is a soft throttle that prefers local region; when local latency > configured SLO or capacity deficit > x%, we reduce local weight and open fallback lanes. Sticky TTL preserves session affinity for a window to keep KV cache hits. Quantization band means we serve a lower-precision model variant in secondary region to preserve throughput.
[00:02:28] Carlos Mendes: when you say quantization band, do you mean reduced token quality? we need to understand regression risk.
[00:02:33] Ethan Park: yes, smaller bit-width or int8 model variants can increase throughput but may change completions subtly — we recommended tying quantization fallbacks to soft regression checks: sample requests from the rolling prompt set and run a lightweight eval before promoting fallback.
[00:02:52] Dr. Priya Rao: ok that evaluation step, is that synchronous? we can't add latency.
[00:02:57] Ethan Park: it's asynchronous. We run it in a canary lane with mirror traffic. If regression > threshold, we pause the fallback. It's a gating signal not a per-request check.
[00:03:08] Maya Chen: practical example — scenario A: regional GPU pool drops to 40% capacity, policy re-routes 30% new sessions to fallback region, maintains sticky TTL of 10 minutes for existing sessions, triggers KV-cache warmup for top prefixes, and spins up quantized instances in fallback region.
[00:03:25] Tom Greer: how do you warm KV without violating privacy — we don't want data replicated cross-region.
[00:03:31] Ethan Park: we only warm public/static prefix keys and metadata; for PHI prefixes we use synthetic warmup (request replay with anonymized tokens) or reconstruct prompts from minimal features. Also you can opt-in to encrypted key sync where the keys are encrypted with customer-managed KMS and only decrypted in-target region.
[00:03:48] [00:04:00] Dr. Priya Rao: mhm, and what's the expected latency hit when you do the 30% shift?
[00:04:06] Maya Chen: great question — depends on network egress and decode bandwidth. In our benchmarks, inter-region fallback to a quantized int8 variant adds ~60–120ms p95 for same-sized prompts, plus an extra 20–40ms if KV misses and we have to pull prefixes. So usually under 200–350ms p95 depending on prompt length.
[00:04:28] Carlos Mendes: that's close to our threshold; we need the ability to opt for partial fallbacks (non-critical flows only).
[00:04:33] Maya Chen: yep, policy routing supports class-based fallback — you can mark routes as critical/soft/metrics-only, and set different penalty thresholds.
[00:04:41] [00:05:00] Ethan Park: about batching — when capacity tightens we recommend switching from latency-first batching to throughput-first with smaller batch packing but more frequent inference calls. There's a balancing act: larger batches are more efficient but increase tail latency. We expose an SLO-preserving auto-mode that tweaks batch size based on observed p95.
[00:05:18] Aisha Khan: any advice on observability? we need traceability of why a particular session got evicted to fallback.
[00:05:23] Maya Chen: yes, console exposes per-request routing decision tags: decision.reason, decision.policy_version, kv.hit_rate, model.variant. You can trace per-session lineage and tie it to audit logs. We'll include recommended retention windows for compliance.
[00:05:38] [00:06:00] Dr. Priya Rao: can we see a sample evacuation runbook? step-by-step, execs want an ordered list.
[00:06:07] Maya Chen: sure, high-level runbook we proposed in the deck: 1) Detect — automated alarms when regional capacity < X% or error rate spike > Y; 2) Notify — send to SRE+Ops and open a checkpoint call; 3) Gradual redirect — change route weights to open fallback lane at low ramp; 4) Warmup — trigger KV warmup and prefix preloads; 5) Promote — increase fallback weight to desired level; 6) Revert — once region healthy, drain without invalidating sessions.
[00:06:33] Ethan Park: addendum: during promote step, mirror 5% of traffic to a canary quantized lane with synchronous metrics so we can watch quality regressions.
[00:06:43] Tom Greer: how long does warmup take realistically?
[00:06:46] Ethan Park: depends on traffic — for top 20 prefixes usually 2–6 minutes; for full working set it's hours. That's why staged warmup matters.
[00:06:56] [00:07:00] Carlos Mendes: are there costs breaking points where this becomes too expensive to run?
[00:07:03] Maya Chen: absolutely — pre-warming is the main cost. Our suggestion is to parametrize warmup size and budget, and only pre-warm the minimal hot set. Also pricing models for Dedicated/Private can include reserved standby capacity to cut on-demand warmup costs.
[00:07:18] Dr. Priya Rao: we also want to ensure runbook steps are executable by our on-call SREs without involving Redwood ops every time.
[00:07:25] Maya Chen: agreed — we hand over runbook playbooks, runbook scripts, and a CLI module to trigger warmup and routing changes which your SRE can use; Ethan will show the scripts.
[00:07:33] [00:08:00] Ethan Park: demoing quick pseudo-CLI: "redwoodctl route adjust --policy evacuation-v1 --add-weight region-us-east=0.3 --sticky-ttl 600 --quantize int8". This emits events to audit log and returns a plan. The KV warmup helper: "redwoodctl kvc warm --prefix-list recent-prefixes.csv --parallelism 8 --anonymize".
[00:08:56] Aisha Khan: anonymize step—what's the algorithm? we can't leak structure.
[00:08:59] Ethan Park: it's a deterministic hash with salt you provide; payloads are masked to remove PHI but maintain prefix structure for warmup effectiveness. We also support synthetic replays from sanitized corpuses.
[00:09:14] [00:09:30] Dr. Priya Rao: ok, switching to decisioning controls — does Redwood allow timed rollbacks? e.g., auto-revert if p95 > target for 10 minutes?
[00:09:37] Maya Chen: yes, rollout policies support conditional automations: promote, observe window, and auto-revert thresholds. You can also configure step sizes for weight shifts.
[00:09:47] Tom Greer: any limits on parallel canaries? we run thousands of sessions, can we canary per-route?
[00:09:52] Ethan Park: you can define canaries per-route or per-customer; we recommend coarse granularity for performance reasons — per-route can be sufficient if routes are well-scoped.
[00:10:02] [00:10:30] Carlos Mendes: one more networking question: our firewall rules are strict, do we need inbound IR or can we pull from within VPC?
[00:10:36] Maya Chen: for private control plane we can run agents in your VPC that orchestrate warmup and routing changes without direct public inbound. Fallback to public regions requires egress rules and approved peering.
[00:10:48] Aisha Khan: legal will want an explicit matrix of what data crosses region and under which keys.
[00:10:52] Maya Chen: we'll include a compliance matrix in the security pack.
[00:10:56] [00:11:30] Ethan Park: small gotcha on KV eviction: when we route sessions to fallback, the local KV segments may still be pinned on the source, so we apply a TTL-driven eviction with controlled spill to prevent double-spend on warmup.
[00:11:45] Dr. Priya Rao: "double-spend"? you mean double charges for warmups?
[00:11:48] Ethan Park: yes, warmup hitting same keys in both regions costs twice — so we try to coordinate via hints in the routing plan to avoid that.
[00:11:55] Maya Chen: reminders: we can avoid dual warmups by prioritizing mirrored warmups to canary lanes first and only full warmups on confirmed route increases.
[00:12:10] [00:12:30] Tom Greer: how do you measure quality regression on quantized models?
[00:12:33] Ethan Park: we use a lightweight eval harness — a mix of unit prompts, prompt-hash similarity, and a small human-in-loop sample for critical flows. The system reports a delta score and flags if beyond threshold.
[00:12:45] Dr. Priya Rao: sample size for canary evaluation?
[00:12:48] Ethan Park: default 200 samples per 1k mirrored requests, configurable.
[00:12:53] [00:13:30] Maya Chen: ok let's run through a simulated evacuation timeline: T0 detect, T+1min notify, T+3min open lane at 5%, T+5min warm top prefixes, T+10min increase lane to 30% if canary metrics within thresholds. Evac is a 15–30min operation for targeted flows.
[00:13:50] Carlos Mendes: sounds reasonable. we like the step model because we can keep triage workflows local as a priority.
[00:13:56] Aisha Khan: any post-evac reconciliation? logs, audit, and model drift checks?
[00:14:01] Maya Chen: yes, a reconciliation job compares mirrored outputs and flags drift. We'll provide a postmortem template.
[00:14:08] [00:14:30] Ethan Park: two operational notes: 1) sticky TTL must be tuned to balance KV hit-rate vs stale affinity, we typically start at 5–10 minutes; 2) route penalty should avoid oscillation — use hysteresis windows.
[00:14:46] Dr. Priya Rao: good. also want a demonstration of a full cold start cost estimate vs reserving a small standby pool.
[00:14:53] Maya Chen: we'll share a cost model spreadsheet — it'll show break-even points for reserved standby capacity.
[00:14:59] [00:15:45] Carlos Mendes: are there any limitations with on-prem hardware? we have mixed A100 and T4 fleets in colo.
[00:15:51] Ethan Park: mixed fleets are fine, runtime will pick kernels appropriate to each device; quantization profiles differ by hardware though, so fallback bands are per-hardware-class. We'll include a mapping.
[00:16:03] Tom Greer: how about network egress costs when we failover to a different cloud region?
[00:16:07] Maya Chen: those are real — egress and cross-region data transfer are billed; cost model includes those and we can show opt-in strategies to minimize transfer by warming only minimal prefixes.
[00:16:18] [00:16:30] Aisha Khan: for compliance we need to be able to wholly prevent some flows from leaving region (e.g., PHI). That means we need a route class with absolute block semantics.
[00:16:38] Ethan Park: supported — you can tag route groups as "no-fallback" and the system will reject attempts to route them out.
[00:16:45] Dr. Priya Rao: ok great. what's the plan to validate this?
[00:16:49] Maya Chen: propose a three-phase validation: 1) tabletop review of runbook and approval (this call), 2) dry-run simulation using synthetic traffic and Canary metrics in a staging environment, 3) live canary under low load followed by progressive ramp. We suggest staging DR exercise first.
[00:17:08] [00:17:30] Ethan Park: quick note on metrics — collect model.latency.p95, kv.hit_rate, decision.reason, fallback.weight, quant.variant, and a quality.delta. All emitted to console and to your Datadog/Prometheus via forwarders.
[00:17:45] Carlos Mendes: can we export raw request payloads to our S3 for offline analysis?
[00:17:50] Maya Chen: yes but we'd recommend sanitized exports; agent or connector can push masked payloads to your bucket.
[00:17:58] [00:18:30] Dr. Priya Rao: I have a question about thawing — after an evacuation, how long until KV cache is "hot" again when traffic returns?
[00:18:38] Ethan Park: depends on traffic growth. If it's your normal working set, backfill warms in minutes for top prefixes, hours for entire set. If you reserved standby capacity, it can be near-instant.
[00:18:52] Tom Greer: what about cold-key detection? like detect new prefixes that cause misses.
[00:18:57] Ethan Park: we tag and surface top missers and auto-prioritize them in warmup.
[00:19:05] [00:19:30] Maya Chen: alright let's annotate responsibilities — I'll send the routing policy examples and cost spreadsheet; Ethan will attach kvc warm script; Aisha will confirm compliance constraints. Any other questions?
[00:19:45] Dr. Priya Rao: one last — what happens if the fallback region also starts degrading? multi-tier failover?
[00:19:52] Ethan Park: supported via tiered fallbacks — primary -> secondary -> degraded-local-quant — but at some point you need to degrade non-critical flows. Our routing policy supports multi-hop fallback chains.
[00:20:07] [00:20:30] Carlos Mendes: thanks, this was very helpful. we'll review and come back with a staging test plan.
[00:20:36] Maya Chen: great, we'll follow up with artifacts. Thanks all.
[00:20:42] [end]
